title: Doubt
hookLine: Thomas doubted and was met, not rejected
tomorrow: what if you pray and feel nothing at all, for months?

cards: Pics or it didn't happen. Every group chat has the friend who wants proof, and the friend who rolls their eyes at them. Thomas was the proof friend.
The other apostles tell him they've seen Jesus alive, and he won't take their word for it. People have nicknamed him Doubting Thomas. So was he wrong?
Inside the Church, the question has two sides, and each one has a real case.

teach.b: Thomas wasn't there when Jesus came. So he sets terms: unless he sees the nail marks and puts his hand in the wound, he won't believe. When Jesus comes back, he doesn't send Thomas away.
He offers the wounds, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "put it into my side; and be not faithless, but believing." Thomas answers, "My Lord, and my God."

One side says: faith is a gift you guard. Jesus adds, "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." The Catechism calls willful doubt, refusing to hold what God has revealed, a sin against faith.
On this view, doubt isn't a hobby. It's a crack to tend before it spreads. The other side says: doubt can be part of the road.
The same Catechism names a different thing, involuntary doubt, the hesitation of someone struggling with objections, and doesn't treat it the same way.
In Mark's Gospel, a father cries out, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief," and Jesus heals his son anyway.
Here's one to tell a friend: John Henry Newman, an English convert later named a saint, wrote that "ten thousand difficulties do not make one doubt." Hard questions aren't the same as walking away.
Both sides keep one thing: Thomas brought his doubt into the room, and it was met.

how: Catholics hear Thomas's story every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some say his words, my Lord and my God, silently when the host is raised at Mass.

o: not being sure, and bringing the question
refusing to believe out of stubbornness

s: John's Gospel calls him Doubting Thomas
the nickname came later; John calls him Thomas, who is called Didymus.
the Catechism treats every kind of doubt the same way
it calls willful doubt a sin against faith, and treats involuntary doubt, struggling with objections, differently.
in Mark, a father says he believes and asks help with his unbelief
I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief.

games.q: at dinner, your aunt says doubt is dangerous and your cousin says doubt is just honest. you side with your cousin. what's your aunt's best case?
o: faith is a gift to guard; Jesus calls blessed those who believe without seeing.
doubters are people who don't go to Mass enough.
the Church bars anyone with doubts from communion.
games.why: her best case is in John 20:29 and the Catechism's warning about willful doubt. the other side has Mark's father and Newman. both agree Thomas's doubt was met.

practice: Sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Bring one real doubt, and set it in your hands instead of hiding it.
If you pray, you can say the father's line, I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief, and keep your hands open while the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: Doubt. Not being sure. In John, the doubter's question gets an answer, not a closed door.

orig.note: Greek, John 20:27: faithless, not believing. Jesus says be not apistos but pistos, believing.

carryVoice: Keep this: doubt was met, because Thomas asked to touch and Jesus held out his hands. Good night.
